newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House tax panel to take up tax cut legislation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House tax panel to take up tax cut legislation.

text.p: The House tax-writing committee was to take the first stab Wednesday at legislation to cut taxes by a net $85 billion over five years with Republicans and Democrats at odds over key provisions.

The House Ways and Means Committee planned to consider a proposal from Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, of how to accomplish the amount of tax cuts agreed to in a budget pact between congressional Republicans and the White House.
The committee meeting on the tax legislation was delayed until 6 p.m. EDT from an initial 11 a.m. EDT schedule.
There was also some last minute tinkering by Archer on a provision to provide inheritance tax relief, which prompted House Speaker Newt Gingrich to say it strengthened the bill.
Archer's legislation included tax incentives for higher education, a child tax credit and a reduction in the capital gains tax.
House Democrats planned to offer an alternative tax bill in the committee.

The Democratic alternative would provide $40 billion over five years for college education tax incentives and $71 billion for a phased-in $500 per child tax credit for children under age 18. Archer's child tax credit would cover children under age 17.
The Democratic plan would provide a more targeted capital gains tax cut than Archer's plan, focusing on small businesses, family farms and real estate.

In addition, the White House continued to put forward new tax proposals. Vice President Al Gore said the White House was proposing two new tax cuts to expand a small business capital gains tax incentive and to expand the home-office tax deduction.

The estate tax change that Archer planned to propose would move $10 billion over 10 years from a proposed phase out of the corporate alternative minimum tax into the estate tax relief portion of his legislation, a committee aide said.

Archer had originally proposed increasing the threshold where estate taxes kick in to $1 million gradually from the current $600,000. Critics had said the initial proposal phased in the higher threshold too gradually because it would reach the $1 million mark in 2014.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said he was "gratified" by Republican plans to modify the alternative minimum tax phase-out proposal, but questioned using the money to offer more estate tax relief.

Representative Jim Nussle, an Iowa Republican, planned to introduce an amendment to strip ethanol language from the tax package. Archer has proposed paring down the tax break supporting production of the corn-based fuel and eliminating it in 2000.

The proposal to reduce the ethanol subsidy raised opposition from lawmakers from farm states and agriculture groups. Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, has previously questioned whether there was currently enough support to eliminate the ethanol subsidy.
Representative Nancy Johnson, a Connecticut Republican, said she planned to offer an amendment to increase the cigarette tax to 53 cents a pack from 24 cents to fund children's health insurance.
